youtube.aciklama:
We explain the basic concepts needed to understand genetic hearing loss: DNA, genes, chromosomes, alleles, genotype and phenotype. With examples, we look at autosomal recessive and dominant, X-linked and mitochondrial inheritance, pedigree symbols, penetrance and variable expressivity.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Thompson and Thompson Genetics in Medicine; Toriello and Smith, Hereditary Hearing Loss and Its Syndromes; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Bennett RL et al., Standardized human pedigree nomenclature, Journal of Genetic Counseling (2008); Hacettepe University Institute of Population Studies, Turkey Demographic and Health Survey 2018.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn the basic concepts needed to understand genetic hearing loss: genes, chromosomes and alleles.
We will look at autosomal dominant and recessive, X-linked and mitochondrial inheritance, and how to read a pedigree.
To understand inheritance, let us first get to know a few basic concepts.
DNA is the molecule that carries hereditary information in our cells; it is like a very long text written in a four-letter alphabet.
A section of this text that codes for a specific task is called a gene; a gene usually carries the recipe for making a protein.
Humans have about twenty thousand genes that code for proteins.
Proteins do the work of the cell; for example, some proteins in the cochlea let potassium ions pass between cells.
If a change in a gene disrupts the structure or amount of a protein, problems can arise in the tissue where that protein works.

maddeler.metin: One from the mother, one _from the father_

cumleler: In the cell nucleus, DNA is packed into bundles called chromosomes.
Humans have forty six chromosomes, that is, twenty three pairs.
One chromosome of each pair comes from the mother and the other from the father.
Twenty two pairs are autosomes, which do not depend on sex; the last pair is the sex chromosomes.
Females have two X chromosomes, and males have one X and one Y chromosome.
Mitochondria, the energy-producing parts of the cell, also have their own small DNA, and this DNA comes from the mother.
Each gene on the autosomes has two copies, one from the mother and one from the father.
The different versions of a gene are called alleles.
If a person's two copies are the same allele, the person is homozygous; if they are different alleles, heterozygous.
The genotype is the combination of alleles a person carries; the phenotype is the visible or measurable result.
In audiology, the phenotype is often the audiogram: the degree of loss, its configuration and its age of onset.
In the genetics literature, changes that cause disease are increasingly called pathogenic variants instead of mutations.
In this lesson, to keep things clear, we will use the terms altered gene and change.

maddeler.metin: Everyone is a _carrier_ of some changes

yan.metin: A person with *one copy* of a recessive allele, usually unaffected

cumleler: Whether one copy of an allele is enough to show its effect determines the pattern of inheritance.
An allele that shows its effect even with a single copy is called a dominant allele.
An allele that needs both copies to show its effect is called a recessive allele.
A person who carries only one copy of a recessive allele is called a carrier; carriers are usually unaffected.
Everyone is a carrier of a few recessive changes; most of us never know it.
In autosomal recessive inheritance, a child must receive two altered copies to be affected.
Most often, the mother and father are hearing carriers; each carries one altered copy and one working copy.
For each child of two such carriers, the chance of being affected is twenty five percent.
The chance that the child is a carrier is fifty percent, and the chance of carrying no altered copy is twenty five percent.
These chances apply anew in every pregnancy; having one affected child does not change the chances for the next.
In a pedigree, recessive conditions often appear in siblings of the same generation and may not appear in earlier generations.
Girls and boys are affected equally often.
On screen you see a simple pedigree; the Roman numerals show the generations.
In the first generation, the double line between the mother and father shows that the partners are related to each other.
Both are carriers of the same altered gene, and both have normal hearing.
In the second generation, one of four children has hearing loss; the filled symbol shows the affected person.
Related partners are more likely to carry the same altered gene from a shared ancestor, so the risk of recessive conditions rises.

cumleler: We will look at consanguinity and genetic counseling in detail in a later lesson.
In autosomal dominant inheritance, a single altered copy is enough to be affected.
Each child of an affected parent has a fifty percent chance of receiving the altered copy.
So in a pedigree, dominant conditions are seen from generation to generation, in a vertical line.
Females and males are affected equally often, and the condition can also pass from father to son.
Nonsyndromic dominant hearing losses usually begin after birth and progress over time.
Sometimes there is no family history at all; the change has newly appeared in the child, and this is called a de novo change.
In X-linked inheritance, the altered gene is on the X chromosome.
Because males have only one X chromosome, an X-linked recessive change shows its effect directly in males.
Thanks to the working copy on their second X chromosome, females are mostly carriers or mildly affected.
For each son of a carrier mother, the chance of being affected is fifty percent.
An affected father cannot pass the change to his sons, but all his daughters will be carriers.
In mitochondrial inheritance, the change passes only from the mother; all children of an affected mother carry the change.
The father's mitochondrial DNA is not passed to the children; we will see a drug-related example in later genetics lessons.
A pedigree is a drawing that shows the people in a family and their relationships with standard symbols.
Squares show males and circles show females; a filled symbol is an affected person.
Partners are joined by a horizontal line; a double line is used between related partners.
Children are shown by a vertical line coming down from this line and are placed from left to right in birth order.
The first person who brings the family to the clinic, the index case or proband, is marked with an arrow.
Generations are numbered with Roman numerals, and people in each generation are numbered from left to right.
In real families, inheritance does not always look as tidy as in the textbook.
Penetrance is the share of people with the change who are actually affected; some carriers show no signs at all.
Variable expressivity means that people with the same change show findings of different severity.
For example, in Waardenburg syndrome, one person in a family may have severe hearing loss and another only a white forelock.
Also, the same hearing loss can come from different genes, and the same gene can show different inheritance patterns.
So family history alone does not give a definite answer; genetic evaluation and counseling are needed.
Genetics is one of the fastest growing areas of audiology.
In developed countries, more than half of congenital hearing losses have a genetic cause.
Today, more than one hundred genes linked to hearing loss have been identified.
Most of these genes work in the cochlea: in the hair cells, in structures that keep the ion balance, and in nerve connections.
Knowing the pattern of inheritance helps estimate the risk for other children in the family.
We will cover syndromic and nonsyndromic losses, the most common genes and genetic counseling in detail in later lessons.

sahneler.metin: Draw relatives whose hearing status is unknown and mark them as unknown. Under affected people, write the age of onset and device use.
cumleler: A useful tip for case history: when drawing a pedigree, do not leave out relatives whose hearing status is unknown.
Draw these people too and note that their status is unknown; unknown is not the same as normal.
Under each affected person's symbol, write the age of onset, whether the loss is in one or both ears, and device use.
Such a pedigree makes genetic evaluation much easier.
Each gene has two copies, one from the mother and one from the father; the different versions of a gene are called alleles.
In autosomal recessive inheritance, each child of two carrier parents has a twenty five percent chance of being affected.
In autosomal dominant inheritance, the chance for each child of an affected parent is fifty percent.
In X-linked inheritance, males are affected more often; mitochondrial changes pass only from the mother.

sahneler.aciklama: In autosomal recessive inheritance, each child of two carriers has a _25 percent_ chance of being affected.

The chance that the child is a carrier is fifty percent.
